scenes.name: Grammys, Óscars, Hall of Fame y el Pulitzer
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.desc: Los grandes premios rechazaron o reconocieron tarde al hip hop. En los Grammy de 1984, la noche de Thriller, Herbie Hancock tocó «Rockit» con Grand Mixer D.ST en los platos: para Paradise Gray, la primera vez que se vio en la tele. En 1989 se creó el Grammy al mejor rap pero se entregó fuera de la retransmisión: Def Jam y Rush encabezaron el boicot y DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince no fueron a recoger el premio por «Parents Just Don’t Understand»; Kool Moe Dee sí fue, harto de que nadie hablara de estrategia («¿no decíamos que nos importaba un carajo el Grammy?»). En 1990 Young MC lo ganó en directo a «Fight the Power» y Flavor Flav le asaltó el escenario. Eminem fue el primer rapero en ganar un Óscar con «Lose Yourself» (2003, con Luis Resto), y Three 6 Mafia el segundo; Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five entraron los primeros en el Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (2007). En 2014 Macklemore se disculpó con Kendrick Lamar por ganarle; en 2018 DAMN. de Lamar, criado en Top Dawg por Punch, ganó el Pulitzer, algo que Nation of Millions habría merecido treinta años antes.

scenes.name: El hip hop: medio siglo de historia oral
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.desc: Un género nacido de la imaginación de chavales abandonados entre las ruinas del Bronx de los setenta que sobrevivió a todo (a una generación mayor que lo rechazaba, a las radios que no lo ponían, a los políticos que lo atacaban) hasta convertirse en la música más popular de Estados Unidos. Abrams hizo más de trescientas entrevistas entre 2018 y 2022 a DJs, artistas, productores, ejecutivos y periodistas para contar su origen y su expansión: del Bronx a los demás distritos «como las venas de un plano del metro», del parque al vinilo, a la Costa Oeste con el gangsta rap y el G-funk, al Sur y más allá. «La lírica es, al fin y al cabo, una forma de tradición oral.»

facts.title: Eurovision Victory (2021)
facts.body: In 2021, Måneskin's surprise win at Eurovision marked a significant moment for rock music, as it brought the title home for rock after years of it primarily going to pop bands. This victory helped propel Måneskin to global recognition and demonstrated rock's continued relevance on an international stage. "Manaskin brought the title home for rock. Not only that, they parlayed their Eurovision win into a global career."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: A 2021 scientific experiment studying metal music and its fans uncovered that metal enthusiasts are among the happiest music fans, ranking second only to jazz fans in terms of overall happiness. "One of the things a 2021 experiment uncovered was that metal fans are among the happiest music fans out there."

facts.title: FBI File Release (2021)
facts.body: In 2021, the FBI made its file on Kurt Cobain publicly available. The file, consisting of only 10 pages, contained letters from two redacted individuals urging the bureau to investigate Cobain's death further. However, the release provided no additional clues or new information that could alter the official suicide ruling. "It was all of 10 pages long. It included letters written to the bureau by two people urging an investigation into Kurt's death."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Daft Punk Breakup (February 22, 2021) – Clip from Electroma; 1993–2021; No Reason Given
facts.body: On February 22, 2021, a clip from their 2006 film Electroma appeared on Daft Punk's YouTube channel — ending with one robot exploding while the other walks away — followed by a title card reading "1993–2021." A spokesperson confirmed the breakup the next day but gave no reason. Thomas Bangalter subsequently released a handwritten note quoting lyrics from "Touch" alongside a clip from Charlie Chaplin's 1936 film Modern Times. Daft Punk released a grand total of four proper studio albums over 28 years. "Daft Punk has gone down in history as one of the most influential bands in the history of dance."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Daft Punk

facts.title: December 2021 Health Scare
facts.body: On December 9, 2021, the Foo Fighters' private jet was bound for Chicago to connect to a flight for Abu Dhabi, where they were scheduled to play the Formula One race season finale. However, a band member, believed to be Taylor Hawkins, had to be rushed to the hospital upon landing in Chicago, allegedly due to exhaustion and dehydration, which was unconfirmed by the band. facts.title: Large B Cell Lymphoma Diagnosis (2021)
facts.body: In June 2021, Mark Hoppus discovered a concerning lump on his shoulder that was quickly diagnosed as stage 4 large B cell lymphoma, a fast-growing cancer type previously experienced by his mother. Terrified and believing he would die, he immediately began intensive chemotherapy. "It was something called large B cell lymphoma. This is a fast growing type of cancer, because the same cancer his mother had, and Mark's was stage 4."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Mark Hoppus

facts.title: Grueling Chemotherapy Experience (2021)
facts.body: Mark Hoppus underwent incredibly strong chemotherapy treatments. During one session, the drugs were so potent that his doctors advised his wife not to share a toilet with him for three days. He likened chemo to "being on the worst international overnight flight where you can't sleep or get comfortable," suffering from hair loss, constant pain, exhaustion, and persistent "brain fog" that made him feel "diminished mentally." "He says, chemo is like being on the worst international overnight flight where you can't sleep or get comfortable."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Mark Hoppus

facts.title: Accidental Public Cancer Revelation (2021)
facts.body: On June 23, 2021, after three months of secrecy, Mark Hoppus accidentally posted a selfie from a chemotherapy infusion to his 1.2 million Instagram followers, instead of his private WhatsApp chat. The photo was captioned, "yes, hello, one cancer treatment, please." Though he deleted it immediately, the news spread, forcing him to issue a public statement confirming his diagnosis and treatment, which he later called "the best mistake I've ever made by far." "Instead, he posted it to Instagram and it went out to 1.2 million followers. It was captioned, yes, hello, one cancer treatment, please."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Mark Hoppus

facts.body: This song, featured on *Saskadelvia*, is not from the *Road Apples* sessions in New Orleans, but was written around 1991. Its lyrics concern the Polytechnique Massacre of 1989. The version on *Saskadelvia* is a live recording from 2000 at the Bell Center in Montreal, performed on an anniversary of the massacre. Guitarist Rob Baker remembered the chords, but Gordon Downie had forgotten the lyrics and needed them printed from a phone provided by a fan just before the encore performance. "I think I had suggested that we do it as an encore, and Gordon was like, yeah, I don't know the words."

facts.body: This album features unreleased material from the band's "glory days of the early 90s," primarily tracks recorded for, but not included on, the 1991 *Road Apples* album. The discovery of these songs, which even the band hadn't heard for decades, was accidental, leading to a "remarkable musical archaeology." The album evokes a sense of Gordon Downie being "in the room" again, as some between-song chatter has been preserved. The album title "Saskadelvia" was an inside joke that the US record company rejected as "too Canadian" for *Road Apples*. The physical packaging includes a front photo from the same session and photographer as *Road Apples*, and a back photo by another photographer involved in the *Road Apples* project, with guitarist Rob Baker credited as "Bobby Baker," reflecting his name in 1991. "enjoyable to hear songs that were so dear to us 30 years ago and 30 years go by and you haven't heard them."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Saskadelvia

facts.body: This song, finally given an official release on *Saskadelvia*, had circulated as a bootleg for decades and was a popular "non-release track" among fans. The band frequently used it as an opening, closing, or encore song in their live sets in 1991 due to its "immediate energy" and "punky" feel. It didn't make the *Road Apples* record possibly because the band felt they had "a better collection of songs" and because producer Don Smith's method of playing songs "over and over and over until we get a killer version," with live guitar solos and vocals, might have fatigued such a high-energy track after multiple takes. "I think we just had a better collection of songs when it came down to count them up."

facts.body: This song, finally given an official release on *Saskadelvia*, had circulated as a bootleg for decades and was a popular "non-release track" among fans. The band frequently used it as an opening, closing, or encore song in their live sets in 1991 due to its "immediate energy" and "punky" feel. It didn't make the *Road Apples* record possibly because the band felt they had "a better collection of songs" and because producer Don Smith's method of playing songs "over and over and over until we get a killer version," with live guitar solos and vocals, might have fatigued such a high-energy track after multiple takes. "I think we just had a better collection of songs when it came down to count them up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Crack My Spine Like A Whip

facts.body: Track five on *Saskadelvia*, this song also circulated as a bootleg for decades and was played live extensively by the band. It has a "country twang" and embodies an "amalgam of blues and country and whatever that became rock and roll." Numerous versions were recorded, and the track "narrowly missed" being included on *Road Apples* when the band was deciding between A and B-side selections. Engineer Bruce Barris can be heard at the beginning of this particular version. "It doesn't really matter so much as it swells. And I guess that's just as well."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Just As Well

facts.body: The sixth and final track on *Saskadelvia*, this is the oldest song on the album, dating back to at least the late 80s. It was among the very first songs the band wrote, originating from a period when Gord Sinclair was the band's "sole songwriter" during their first year and a half as they tried to blend original material into cover band sets. Later, the band evolved beyond individual songwriting. Lyrically, it is seen by band members as "proof positive why we put Gord and charge the lyrics in the band." "Gord was basically our soul songwriter."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Reform Baptist Blues

facts.body: Olivia Rodrigo's debut solo single, a breakup song released in 2021. Listeners speculated its lyrics contained hints about a love triangle involving other Disney actors, creating a "perfect storm for TikTok" due to the mystery and catchy nature of the song. Within three days, it topped all streaming charts, soon reaching the Billboard Hot 100, and became the fastest song ever to hit 100 million listens on Spotify, largely due to its viral success on TikTok. "Everyone was like, I'm crying about these teens that I know nothing about. And now I love this song."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Decoder Ring - The New Age Hit Machine
